questions.q: Which of these are reasons a program might use dynamic memory allocation?
choices: The size of an array is not known until runtime (e.g. it depends on user input)
The program must handle a variety of input sizes, not just up to some fixed capacity
The program wants to allocate exactly the size needed for a particular run without wasting capacity
The program needs to grow or shrink allocated memory as it runs
The program wants memory that is automatically released when the function returns
The program needs a place to store its machine instructions
questions.explain: Dynamic allocation lets a program size data structures at runtime, handle varying input sizes, avoid wasted capacity, and grow or shrink memory as needed. Heap memory is NOT automatically released; it must be explicitly freed. Instructions live in the code region.

questions.q: From which region of a program's memory space does dynamically allocated memory come?
choices: Code
Data
Stack
Heap
questions.explain: Dynamically allocated memory comes from the heap. Code holds instructions, data holds globals, and the stack holds locals and parameters.

questions.q: In which region of program memory do global variables reside?
choices: Code
Data
Stack
Heap
questions.explain: Global variables reside in the data region.

questions.q: In which region of program memory do local variables and function parameters live?
choices: Code
Data
Stack
Heap
questions.explain: Local variables and parameters occupy the stack.

questions.q: Why are the stack and the heap typically placed far apart in a program's address space?
choices: Both grow at runtime, so separating them leaves lots of room for each to grow
So that the heap can be read-only while the stack is writable
Because the stack holds global variables and must be isolated from the heap
Because the compiler needs the gap to store the program's instructions
questions.explain: The stack grows and shrinks as functions are called and return, and the heap grows as memory is allocated and freed. Keeping them far apart gives each a large amount of space to grow into.

questions.q: Heap memory is "anonymous" memory: addresses in the heap are not bound to variable names.
questions.explain: Heap locations have no variable names. A program reaches them only through a pointer variable (local or global) that stores a heap address.

questions.q: Inside a function, the declaration `int *p;` allocates the variable p itself on the heap.
questions.explain: Declaring a named variable allocates it on the stack (for locals) or in the data region (for globals). The local pointer p lives on the stack; it can store the address of heap memory, but p itself is not on the heap.

questions.q: What argument do you pass to malloc?
choices: The total number of bytes of contiguous heap memory to allocate
The number of elements to allocate, regardless of their type
The name of the pointer variable that should receive the memory
The address in the heap where memory should be allocated
questions.explain: malloc takes the total number of bytes to allocate, typically computed with the sizeof operator.

questions.q: What does malloc return if it cannot satisfy the request?
choices: NULL
0 bytes of memory at a valid address
The address of the stack
questions.explain: malloc returns the base address of the allocated memory on success, or NULL if an error occurs.

questions.q: What is the return type of malloc? (Write the C type.)
questions.explain: malloc returns a void *, a generic pointer to an unspecified type. Assigning it to a typed pointer variable associates the memory with that type.

questions.q: malloc and free are part of which standard C library (header)?
questions.explain: malloc and free are in the standard C library stdlib, included with #include <stdlib.h>.

questions.q: In `p = (int *) malloc(sizeof(int));`, what does the `(int *)` do?
choices: Recasts malloc's void * return value so it is used as an int *
Tells malloc to allocate memory on the stack instead of the heap
Multiplies the requested size by sizeof(int *)
Initializes the allocated int to zero
questions.explain: The (int *) explicitly recasts malloc's void * return type to int *, matching the type of the pointer variable p.

choices: It dereferences p without checking whether malloc returned NULL, so a failed malloc would crash the program
malloc(sizeof(int)) allocates memory on the stack, so *p = 6 is invalid
It must cast the result to (int *) or it will not compile
sizeof(int) is the wrong size; it should be sizeof(int *)
questions.explain: Any call to malloc can fail, so you should always test its return value for NULL before dereferencing. Dereferencing a NULL pointer crashes the program.

questions.q: Which of these commonly cause a call to malloc to fail?
choices: Passing malloc a very large request
Passing malloc a negative number of bytes
Calling malloc in an infinite loop until heap memory runs out
Not casting malloc's return value to the pointer's type
Allocating space for chars instead of ints
questions.explain: malloc fails when there isn't enough free heap memory to satisfy the request, which usually indicates a bug such as a very large request, a negative size, or calling malloc in an infinite loop. Casting is optional, and the element type doesn't matter.

questions.q: Heap memory must be explicitly deallocated by the C program (by calling free) when it is no longer needed.
questions.explain: Heap memory must be explicitly allocated with malloc and explicitly deallocated with free by the program.

questions.q: Why is it a good idea to write `p = NULL;` right after `free(p);`?
choices: If p is accidentally dereferenced later, the program crashes immediately instead of silently modifying heap memory that a later malloc may have reallocated
free does not actually release the memory until the pointer is set to NULL
Setting p to NULL returns the memory to the stack
It lets the next call to malloc reuse the same pointer variable without a cast
questions.explain: Using a freed pointer can modify reallocated heap memory and cause undefined behavior that is very hard to debug. A NULL pointer dereference fails immediately, making the bug easy to find and fix.

questions.q: Which call correctly allocates a heap array of 50 doubles?
choices: malloc(sizeof(double) * 50)
malloc(50)
malloc(sizeof(double))
malloc(sizeof(double) + 50)
questions.explain: Request the total number of bytes: the size of each element times the number of elements, in the form sizeof(<type>) * <number of elements>.

questions.q: On a system where sizeof(int) is 4, how many bytes does `malloc(sizeof(int) * 20)` request?
questions.explain: sizeof(int) * 20 = 4 * 20 = 80 bytes.

questions.q: The elements of an array allocated by a single call to malloc are stored in contiguous memory locations.
questions.explain: A successful malloc allocates one contiguous chunk of heap memory, so the array elements are contiguous, just like a statically declared array.

questions.q: Two separate calls to malloc will (on most systems) return heap chunks that are right next to each other in memory.
questions.explain: Multiple calls to malloc will not result in contiguous heap addresses on most systems; the chunks may be far apart in the heap.

questions.q: After `arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * 20);` succeeds, what does the pointer variable arr contain?
choices: Only the base (starting) address of the 20-int block in the heap
A copy of all 20 int values
The size of the block, 20 * sizeof(int)
The address of the last element in the block
questions.explain: The pointer variable (stored on the stack here) holds only the base address of the array storage space in the heap.
d_array[i] accesses the ith element just like a static array. Element 5 was set to 5 * 2 = 10.

questions.q: Which statement has exactly the same effect as `d_array[0] = 8;`?
choices: *d_array = 8;
d_array = 8;
&d_array = 8;
*d_array[0] = 8;
questions.explain: Placing * in front of a pointer to a dynamically allocated array dereferences it to access element 0.

questions.q: Given `int s_array[20];` and `int *d_array = malloc(sizeof(int) * 20);`, which statement is correct?
choices: Both names evaluate to the base address of their array, but s_array's type is a (static) array of int while d_array's type is int *
Both have type int *, and both arrays live on the heap
s_array evaluates to the first element's value while d_array evaluates to an address
They have the same type, but only s_array can be indexed with [i]
questions.explain: Their types differ, but both evaluate to the base address of the array. That's why [i] means the same thing for both: dereference the int at offset i from the base address.

questions.q: The heap memory manager keeps a list of unallocated extents of heap memory. What is this list called?
questions.explain: The heap memory manager maintains a free list of unallocated extents of heap memory.

questions.q: In the heap memory manager's free list, what does each extent specify?
choices: The start address and size of a contiguous unallocated chunk of heap space
The name of the variable that owns a chunk of heap space
The stack frame that allocated a chunk of heap space
The type of data stored in an allocated chunk
questions.explain: Each extent records the start address and size of a contiguous unallocated chunk of heap memory.

questions.q: Before any calls to malloc, the free list has a single extent consisting of the entire heap region.
questions.explain: Initially all of heap memory is empty, so the free list has one extent covering the whole heap.

questions.q: After many calls to malloc and free, chunks of free heap space end up interspersed with chunks of allocated space. What is the heap said to be?
questions.explain: Free chunks interspersed with allocated chunks means the heap has become fragmented.

questions.q: free is passed only an address, not a size. How does it know how many bytes to deallocate?
choices: malloc stores a header with metadata such as the size right before the allocated chunk, and free reads it
free scans forward until it finds a NULL byte marking the end of the chunk
The compiler records each allocation's size in the pointer variable's type
free always deallocates a fixed-size block, regardless of the original request
questions.explain: malloc allocates a few extra bytes just before the chunk for a header that stores metadata such as the size. free gets the size from that header.

questions.category: Pointers to heap memory and functions
questions.q: When main calls `init_array(arr1, 10);` where arr1 points to a malloc'd array, what does init_array's parameter receive?
choices: The value of arr1: the base address of the array in the heap
A full copy of the array's 10 elements, placed on the stack
A newly malloc'd copy of the array
The address of the variable arr1 itself
questions.explain: The pointer's value (the base address) is passed. The array's block of contiguous memory stays on the heap, and the function reaches it by dereferencing its pointer parameter.

questions.category: Pointers to heap memory and functions
questions.q: Why does `void init_array(int *arr, int size)` take a separate size parameter?
choices: Only the base address of the array is passed, so the function needs to be told how many elements to access
Because free requires the size when the function returns
Because malloc must be called again inside the function with that size
Because int * parameters cannot be indexed without a size
questions.explain: Passing the array passes only its base address, so the size is passed separately to tell the function how many elements to access.

questions.category: Pointers to heap memory and functions
questions.q: As function parameter declarations, `int *arr` and `int arr[]` are equivalent.
questions.explain: They are equivalent. By convention, the pointer syntax is often used for functions that may be called with dynamically allocated arrays.

questions.category: Pointers to heap memory and functions
questions.q: The same function can be used for both a statically declared int array and a dynamically allocated int array.
questions.explain: In both cases the parameter gets the same kind of value, the base address of the array, so the same function and the same [i] syntax work for both.

questions.category: Pointers to heap memory and functions
questions.q: Just before init_array returns, how are main's arr1 and init_array's arr related?
choices: Both store the same base address and point to the same block of heap memory
arr points to a separate copy of the array that init_array made on the heap
arr points to a copy of the array on the stack, and arr1 points to the heap
arr stores the address of arr1, which is on main's stack frame
questions.explain: Both pointer variables hold the same base address, so changes made through arr (like arr[i] = i) are visible through arr1 in main.
